source.title: Understanding Generalization through Visualizations
source.authors: W. R. Huang; Z. Emam; Micah Goldblum; Liam H. Fowl; J. K. Terry; Furong Huang; T. Goldstein

record.file_problem: The supplied text appears to contain the full paper.
record.tranche_reason: The study uses experiments and visualizations to relate loss-landscape flatness and basin volume to generalization, using a different measurement approach from the magnitude-aware sharpness comparison in V7.
record.gate_note: The paper cites prior work on fitting random labels but does not report its own random-label experiment. Its own optimizer comparison is described qualitatively, with plotted values in Figure 2. Poisoned training deliberately induces poor test performance, so those results do not test V1's random-label condition.
record.test_reason: Figure 2 directly compares adaptive optimizers with SGD variants on VGG13/CIFAR-10, bearing on V4. However, the supplied text does not reveal their relative accuracies or tuning protocol, so no directional verdict is justified. The poisoned-minimum experiments do not establish V7's specified magnitude-aware training-error measure.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors offer visual and experimental intuition connecting generalization, flatness, and basin volume, and suggest that high dimensionality biases optimization toward good minima. They leave invariant volume definitions, attraction basins, and rigorous generalization guarantees unresolved.
record.recipe_differences: Uses standard SGD and a poisoning procedure to compare minima, then visualizes loss landscapes and basin volumes; it does not reproduce the magnitude-aware perturbation-ranking procedure described in V7.
record.method_sensitivity: Poison factor changes test accuracy and the observed sharpness/generalization relationship. The optimizer comparison reports performance differences, but the supplied text gives no per-optimizer values.

fits_no_version.finding: Standard and poisoned SVHN minima both achieve 100% training accuracy, but reach 97.1% and 28.2% test accuracy respectively; filter-normalized loss slices show the latter is sharper.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Deliberately induced poor generalization can coincide with sharper filter-normalized loss landscapes.

fits_no_version.finding: The swissroll networks both fit training data perfectly, while standard and poisoned training yield 100% and 7% test accuracy; the poisoned solution has smaller margins and a sharper loss slice.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Poisoned fully connected classifiers can have small decision margins and sharp local loss geometry.

fits_no_version.finding: ResNet-18 and a similarly sized linear classifier both fit CIFAR-10 training data perfectly but achieve 92% and 49% test accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Comparable parameter counts and perfect training accuracy do not determine comparable generalization across model classes.

fits_no_version.finding: Section 5 reports shrinking basin radii as poisoning increases the generalization gap, with good SVHN basins at least 10,000 orders of magnitude larger than bad basins.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under a poisoning sweep, low-loss basin radius and estimated volume correlate with generalization.

record.problems: Small numbers of optimizer runs are reported for basin-radius statistics (10 for swissroll and 4 for SVHN); sharpness comparisons are visual/qualitative. The paper itself says experiments raise questions and that the correct invariant definition of volume and attraction basins remains unresolved.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted. The paper cites random-label fitting by Zhang et al. and related work, but those cited results are not this study's own results.

untested.parts: No own random-label fitting and held-out comparison against natural-label training.
No width sweep beyond the width required for interpolation.
No convolutional-versus-fully-connected neural-network comparison or test of learned local connectivity.
Limited versus broader tuning, language benchmarks, decoupled weight decay, and switching optimizers are not established.
No batch-size comparison under fixed epoch budgets or adapted training recipes.
No evaluation of the specified magnitude-aware training-error tolerance or its ranking against norm- and margin-based measures among ordinarily trained convolutional networks.
No removal of memorized examples followed by retraining.

missing.what: Readable per-optimizer training and test accuracies, together with the learning-rate, schedule, and other tuning protocol, are needed to resolve the V4 comparison. Existing rows contain placeholders rather than those results.

record.verdict_notes: No listed original source is this study. All optimizer methods outperforming the linear classifier does not establish their ordering against SGD. The supplied figure text lacks the plotted values, so neither support nor challenge to V4 can be assigned.

versions.untested_parts: Does not report fitting random labels or compare natural-label and random-label held-out accuracy using the same architecture and training recipe.
No width sweep beyond the interpolation threshold.
Does not compare convolutional and fully connected networks on images.
Does not report an adaptive-versus-SGD comparison under the version's limited-tuning conditions.

Does not test the specified network family and datasets, compare against the named norm- and margin-based measures, or establish that sharpness predicts gaps across a broad set of similarly trained networks.
Does not remove memorized training examples and retrain.

rows.subject: ResNet-18
rows.operation_detail: Compared flatness of standard-trained and poisoned-trained minima with test accuracy using loss-landscape visualizations.
rows.measure: Training and test accuracy; relative sharpness in loss-landscape visualization.
rows.value: The good minimizer is flat and achieves 97.1% test accuracy; the bad minimizer is much sharper and achieves 28.2% test accuracy. Both achieve 100% train accuracy.
rows.note: The comparison changes the poison factor; the paper describes the good and bad minima as having identical hyperparameters apart from that factor. It does not report a numerical sharpness score.
rows.check: The accuracies are correct, but filter-normalized two-dimensional loss slices do not measure V7's perturbation tolerance before training error rises. Poor generalization is deliberately induced by the poisoning objective.

rows.subject: 6-layer fully connected neural network
rows.operation_detail: Compared decision-boundary margins and loss-landscape sharpness for a standard-trained minimizer and a poisoned minimizer.
rows.measure: Training and test accuracy; qualitative margin and loss-landscape flatness.
rows.value: The good network has 100% train and 100% test accuracy; the bad network has 100% train and 7% test accuracy. The bad minimizer is described as sharp, while the good minimizer has a wide basin.
rows.note: Sharpness is shown qualitatively; no numeric sharpness measure is reported.
rows.check: The reported accuracies are correct. This fully connected swissroll experiment does not test V7's convolutional-family claim or specified sharpness measure; poor generalization is deliberately induced.

rows.subject: ResNet-18
rows.operation_detail: Trained on CIFAR-10 using SGD; the paper reports training and test accuracy.
rows.value: Perfect training accuracy and 92% test accuracy.
rows.note: Compared with a linear model of comparable parameter count. This does not test the version's random-label condition.
rows.check: Accuracies are correctly reported, but natural-label fitting alone does not test V1. The comparator is a linear model, not a fully connected neural network as required by V3.

rows.subject: Linear model with pixel intensities and pair-wise products of pixel intensities
rows.operation_detail: Trained on CIFAR-10 using SGD; the paper reports training and test accuracy.

conditions.value: images downsampled by a factor of 2 before pair-wise products

rows.value: Perfect training accuracy and 49% test accuracy.
rows.note: Comparator to the ResNet-18 with a comparable parameter count. Does not test the version's random-label condition.
rows.check: Accuracies are correctly reported. This linear classifier with engineered quadratic features does not test V3's fully connected neural-network comparison or V1's random-label condition.

reader_labels.reason: At identical train accuracy, the text describes the well-generalizing minimizer as flat and the poor-generalizing minimizer as much sharper (R1). This is qualitative evidence of the relation.

reader_labels.label: supports
